Q138869462.summary: Christ, seen from behind, rises up a channel of cloud and grasps the hand of God reaching down from heaven, while rows of figures look on from the clouds at either side. Below, two angels gesture down to the Virgin and the apostles, who crowd together in vivid gestures of wonder. Framed by a deep acanthus border, this ivory once adorned the cover of a liturgical book, presenting the Ascension as the triumphant return of the Son to the Father.
facts: The Kunsthistorisches Museum dates the plaque to the end of the 10th century and attributes it, with a query, to Metz.
The museum notes that the elegant acanthus frieze and parts of the composition follow Byzantine models.
Showing Christ from behind being drawn up by the hand of God is a distinctive Western way of representing the Ascension.
Q138869462.notes: Inv. Kunstkammer 7284; 20.6 × 14.4 cm. Date was '900s'; the museum gives 'Ende 10. Jh.'. The third fact is a general iconographic observation, not from the museum text.

cur:monumental-santa-prassede-triumphal-.summary: Across the top of the triumphal arch, the walls of the heavenly Jerusalem enclose a company of saints, at whose centre Christ stands between angels; outside the gates further crowds of the elect, led by angels, approach to enter. Below, the apsidal arch and the apse itself continue the vision with the Lamb, the elders and Christ in glory. The arch is one of the most elaborate images of the heavenly city in medieval Rome.
facts: Paschal I (817–824) employed a team of professional mosaicists to decorate the apse, the apsidal arch and the triumphal arch of the church he rebuilt.
Paschal I's mosaics belong to the Carolingian-era revival in Rome, when the pope also translated many martyrs' relics from the catacombs into the city's churches.

cur:monumental-santa-prassede-triumphal-.notes: The photograph shows the whole sanctuary; the scene described is on the outer (triumphal) arch at the top. The apse mosaic is a separate entry in the collection.

cur:objects-durrow-high-cross.summary: Standing now inside the old church at Durrow, this high cross shows at the centre of its ringed head the crucified Christ, arms stretched along the cross-arms and surrounded by small figures. The shaft below is covered with panels of figures and interlace. Durrow, famous for its gospel book, was one of the great Columban monasteries, and its cross placed Christ's saving death before the community's eyes.
facts: Wikipedia lists among the monuments at Durrow Abbey 'a mid-ninth century high cross', and counts Durrow with Kells and Monasterboice among the sites of the 'classic' Irish high crosses.

walters:71.163.summary: A small seated Virgin, wearing her original gilt-copper crown, raises her hand to the standing Christ Child, who stands lightly on her lap and reaches up to touch her veil. The drapery falls in crisp, geometric folds, and the Child is unusually thin and lively. The group, only 11 cm high, captures the affectionate exchange between mother and son.
facts: The Walters notes that the gilt-copper crown is original, and that the bone support beneath is probably 18th-century Scandinavian work.
It was sold with the A. André collection in Paris in 1920 and passed through the Paris dealer Léon Gruel before Henry Walters bought it in 1922.
walters:71.163.notes: Worklist year 850 was a parsing error for '4th quarter 14th century'. The Child's left arm is broken.
